paras: The lynching of Dennis Williams took place at Ellaville, Florida, in June 1888, when a mob took Williams, a Black man accused of shooting a mill superintendent, from the men guarding him and killed him. His body was found in the Suwanee River riddled with bullets. The story ran in papers across the country as a short Tallahassee dispatch, which added that Black residents were reported to be planning revenge.

Ellaville was described as a lumber depot some thirty miles east of Tallahassee. According to an Ellaville dispatch, on Saturday night, June 9, Superintendent William McCormick ordered Williams to hand over a gun that he carried "against orders"; Williams told him to stand back and, when McCormick demanded the gun again, fired. A later account said Williams had held the loaded gun "in a threatening manner in a crowd of people" and that McCormick tried to take it from him. The bullet struck McCormick in the right shoulder and shattered the bone.
McCormick was described as "very popular," and the shooting "created immense excitement."

Williams was pursued, caught and locked in a smoke-house that was "closely guarded." Early the next morning, June 10, the guards were found gagged and bound and the smoke-house empty; the True Northerner said they had been bound "by the lynchers." At first it was thought that Williams's friends had freed him, but on the morning of June 11 his body was found in the Suwanee River, "riddled with bullets and his head badly smashed."

The Tallahassee wire gave a shorter version: Williams "was taken to the woods by a mob and lynched yesterday," and his body was afterward found in the river. A variant dispatch said he was lynched on Monday and his body thrown into the river. A brief that circulated in a "Southern Gleanings" column later in the month said the body was "perforated with bullets and having a rope around the neck," a detail the Ellaville dispatch did not mention.

The Tallahassee wire reported that "the negroes are greatly incensed" and would try to avenge the lynching. A week later the True Northerner repeated a rumor that Black residents had "banded together for revenge," but no report of an outbreak follows in the coverage. No arrest of the lynchers, inquest or report on McCormick's recovery appears in the coverage.

The New York Sun printed the fullest account, an Ellaville dispatch headed "Lynch Law in Florida," on June 12. The same day the Tallahassee wire appeared in the Washington Evening Star, the Alexandria Gazette and the San Antonio Daily Light, the last under the heading "Trouble With the Negroes." Over the next week it was reprinted in Wheeling, Indianapolis, Michigan, Maysville, Springfield, Mississippi and Rhode Island, often under "A Negro Lynched" or "Taken to the Woods and Lynched."

Some headlines took the lynchers' side: the Sun's second notice called Williams "a Colored Criminal," and the News-Herald in Ohio ran the wire under "It Was Not Murder." The True Northerner headed its summary "Dennis Williams Hanged by a Mob for Wounding a White Man." As the item was condensed for weekly papers in Kansas and West Virginia, the place became "Ellersville" or even Tallahassee. Every report came from white papers, and none gave an account from Williams's side beyond the rumors of revenge.

The Ellaville dispatch dates the removal from the smoke-house to the night before June 10 and the finding of the body to June 11, while the Tallahassee wire puts the lynching itself on June 11. Accounts of the manner of death also differ: the Sun reported bullets and a smashed head, the "Southern Gleanings" item bullets and a rope around the neck.

reader.title: Lynching of Dennis Williams
bases: Every account says Dennis Williams was taken from a guarded smoke-house or 'taken to the woods by a mob' and killed, his body found in the river (A1, A3, A14).

Williams was killed after being seized from the men guarding him by what the wire called 'a mob' and the True Northerner called 'the lynchers', with no lawful authority, in retaliation for his alleged shooting of Superintendent McCormick (A1, A3, A14).

The Ellaville dispatch in the New York Sun and the separate Tallahassee wire agree that Williams was seized after the shooting and his body found in the river, and a later summary and a 'Southern Gleanings' item repeat it (A1, A3, A14, A18).

accounts.label: Ellaville dispatch (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: McCormick was shot after twice demanding a gun Williams carried against orders; Williams was caught and locked in a guarded smoke-house, the guards were found gagged and bound, and his body was found in the Suwanee riddled with bullets and his head smashed; at first his friends were thought to have freed him.

accounts.label: Tallahassee wire
accounts.gist: Williams was taken to the woods by a mob and lynched; his body was found in the river; Black residents were said to be incensed and planning revenge.

accounts.label: Later summary (True Northerner)
accounts.gist: The lynchers bound the guards; the shooting followed McCormick's attempt to take a loaded gun Williams held 'in a threatening manner in a crowd'; a rumor said Black residents had banded together for revenge.

accounts.label: 'Southern Gleanings' column
accounts.gist: Williams was lynched for shooting at a white man; his body was found in the Suwannee perforated with bullets and with a rope around the neck.

framing.detail: The Sun headed its Ellaville dispatch 'Lynch Law in Florida' and gave the shooting and the killing in plain narrative.
Most papers reprinted the Tallahassee wire under 'A Negro Lynched' or similar headings, stressing the threat of Black retaliation ('Trouble With the Negroes').
The Sun's second notice was headed 'Lynched a Colored Criminal', and the News-Herald ran the wire under 'It Was Not Murder.'
The True Northerner headed its summary 'Dennis Williams Hanged by a Mob for Wounding a White Man', naming the race of both men.
